units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And if I have more than a day, or I'm bored of cobblestones?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then you go and look at three other Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The first is Art Nouveau. In the eighteen-nineties, a young architect named Victor Horta built a townhouse for a professor called Emile Tassel, with iron columns shaped like plant stems, stairs that curl like vines, and light pouring down from above.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1893 and 1894, widely regarded as the first Art Nouveau building.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Several of Horta's houses are now UNESCO World Heritage.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Horta Museum is in his own house.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In Saint-Gilles, where he lived and worked.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: If you want one museum, I'd pick that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Comics. A young Brussels cartoonist named Georges Remi, who signed his work Hergé, published the first adventure of a young reporter with a quiff of red hair in a children's supplement in January of 1929.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Belgium's comic strip tradition has made Brussels a world capital of the form.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'll find big comic murals on the sides of buildings around the center, if you keep your eyes up.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The European quarter. If you take the metro to Schuman station and walk out, you'll face the Berlaymont, the star-shaped headquarters of the European Commission.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's not charming in the way the Grand Place is, but it tells you what the city is for now.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A slightly different kind of landmark.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A different kind, and every bit as much part of the story.
